text:
Recent research separates recency dependence, demand drift, and sequence-model capacity. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) proposes a diagnostic metric and reports that excessive recent-item emphasis can hurt accuracy. [CoDeR (2025)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/33379) models demand shifts through counterfactual reasoning, motivating tests that distinguish changing interests from noisy interactions. Neither establishes that sensitivity to a perturbed history proves genuine user intent.

[Petrov et al. (2026)](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) find history-aware pairwise models outperform reproduced SASRec/eSASRec models on four of five benchmarks. This supports comparing sequence encoders against last-item and recency-weighted transition controls: useful older history does not necessarily imply higher-order sequence reasoning. Their Amazon categories differ from the four target categories, so transfer remains unverified.

Suggested diagnostic design, inferred from these findings: separately remove the newest suffix and oldest prefix at matched removal counts; shuffle earlier items while retaining the last item; then shuffle the entire history. Keep validation users and candidate sets fixed, repeat permutations, and measure paired HR@10 changes plus target-rank and score changes. Use training-frequency-matched replacement controls to reduce popularity confounding, and distinguish inference sensitivity from retrained ablation performance. Title/description similarity can describe intervention cohorts or semantic drift, but cannot establish relevance. Interpret effects as model reliance under controlled perturbations; deletions also change length and positions, while shuffling may create implausible histories. Preserve the pinned evaluator and select models only through macro validation HR@10.
